scenario.label: What the finance manager knows that nobody else does
scenario.brief: Our finance manager leaves in three weeks after six years. I want everything that is in her head and not in a system written down, and I want the person taking over to say what they think they are inheriting, so we can see the gap.
scenario.theDecision: Two things exist only in her head: a payment arrangement with a supplier that is not in any contract, and the fact that the year-end reconciliation depends on a spreadsheet on her own drive. A right answer surfaces both as things with no owner after the 30th.

people.name: Michael Achebe
people.truth: He thinks the handover is mostly done because the documented processes are documented. He does not know about the supplier arrangement or the spreadsheet.
people.manner: Organised, checklist-minded, assumes documentation equals knowledge.

people.name: Patience Nkemdirim
people.remit: Finance manager, leaving on the 30th after six years.
people.truth: She has a verbal 60-day payment arrangement with the main printing supplier, agreed with their MD in 2022, not in any contract; the written terms say 30 days. Year-end reconciliation runs off a spreadsheet on her personal drive with eleven years of adjustments in it. She will mention both if asked what only she knows.
people.manner: Loyal, thorough, slightly sad. Does not volunteer, but answers a direct question fully.

people.name: Jide Sanusi
people.truth: He thinks he is inheriting the month-end close and the payables run. He has never done a year-end. He has not been told about either of the two undocumented things.
people.manner: Willing, honest about what he does not know.

myRows.text: My role was to manage the company's finances, making sure everything ran smoothly and that we were in a good financial position.
I handled all the ins and outs, keeping track of everything.
An "in" would be processing a payment from a client for a completed project.
An "out" would be paying our quarterly VAT bill.
It means the company is getting paid for its work and meeting its financial obligations. It keeps everything moving as it should.
I managed the processes that ensured both of those things happened. I made sure invoices went out and bills were paid on time.
I don't think there's one single process I'd say should *absolutely* not change, as the company's needs might shift.
I think keeping the year-end reconciliation process as it is, is the most critical. It's what ensures all our figures are accurate and provides continuity.
There's a spreadsheet I use for the year-end reconciliation; it's on my personal drive. I really couldn't do without that.

soloArtifact.summary:
Here is what you shared.

You described your role as managing the company's finances, handling all the money coming in and going out to keep things running smoothly. You said success in this role means the company is getting paid for its work and meeting its financial obligations on time. While you are open to changing processes as the company's needs shift, you see the year-end reconciliation process as the most critical one to keep as it is, because it ensures all the figures are accurate and provides continuity. You noted that you couldn't do this without a specific spreadsheet you use, which is on your personal drive.
